content.thinking: I should fix the citation to reference AL1 only, replace the "24 hours" figure with the correct placeholder value, and keep the replica count as is, consolidating everything into a single call.

action_items.item: Configure automatic horizontal scale-out for the io-shop deployment, driven by CPU use, so a traffic ramp adds replicas before requests queue.
Add an alert on io-shop CPU use nearing its limit and on a sustained rise in request volume, so saturation pages before p95 latency does.
Add a load test that exercises the account-page spend calculations with long purchase histories and fails when CPU cost per request grows faster than linearly.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw slow responses. p95 latency went from {series_before} before the onset to {series_while_broken} on average, and {series_at_worst} at its worst, for {duration}. Failed requests did not rise beyond normal variation, so the harm was waiting rather than errors.

Requests were waiting in a queue for CPU. The metrics Argus read show request volume ramping and the service reaching its CPU limit, after which latency climbed. Once capacity was added, the service was no longer at the incident's level.

Capacity was fixed while demand grew. The deployment stayed at {T19.2} replicas and had nothing to add capacity under load. Scaling it out confirmed the mitigation and the paging rule stopped firing. Ruled out as the trigger: no production changes in the {T8.2} hours before the onset, and no recent flag changes at the flag provider. The trigger was the traffic ramp alone.

Each request used far more CPU than its result needed, so a ramp that a cheaper request would absorb used up the budget. This comes from Code-Fix's reading of the source only. Nothing ran it, so it is unverified. The reading is that the default account-page spend figure recomputed a running sum for every index and the rollout figure removed the minimum from a list repeatedly. Both are quadratic in the length of a shopper's history.

contributing_factors.factor: The deployment ran on fixed capacity with no automatic scale-out seen in the record. A traffic ramp could therefore saturate CPU until a person or Argus added replicas.

No alert on CPU approaching its limit or on the traffic ramp was seen. The only page seen was the latency rule, which waits {rule_waits} with its condition holding. Saturation had begun before it fired.
Automatic sync of io-shop is off, so nothing merged reaches production until it is turned back on. The CPU-cost fix is also still an unmerged draft.
No load or scaling test of the account-page calculations on long purchase histories was seen, so the quadratic cost reached production unnoticed.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, from {began} to {back_to_normal}, the io-shop pages loaded slowly. The p95 response time was {series_before} before the onset. It averaged {series_while_broken} during the incident and peaked at {series_at_worst}. Shoppers waited much longer for pages, but the error rate did not rise beyond its normal variation: {errors_while_broken} while broken against {errors_before} before. Request volume had climbed until the service ran out of CPU and requests queued. No deploy or flag change was involved. Argus added replicas, and latency returned to normal. A draft pull request has been proposed to cut the CPU cost of each request, and it is not yet merged.

got_lucky: Failed requests did not rise beyond normal variation, so the slowdown did not turn into errors for shoppers.
went_well: The Investigator placed the onset from the metrics and found no production or flag changes, which pointed to demand.
Scaling out was confirmed against the service's own metrics, and the paging rule stopped firing.
Code-Fix proposed a draft fix with deterministic tests that count work rather than time it.
went_wrong: The Investigator did not read logs, so the per-request CPU cost rests on a static reading only.
Automatic sync is off, so a merged fix would not reach io-shop until AI-3 is done.
The deployment had no automatic scale-out seen, so recovery depended on a manual scale-out action.

input.root_cause: Traffic to io-shop ramped up until the fixed CPU allowance of its replicas ran out, and requests queued for CPU. Nothing was deployed or changed. A static reading of the code, which nobody ran, suggests each account-page request did far more CPU work than needed because of quadratic loops in the spend calculations. That reading is unverified. Scaling out cleared the saturation.
input.symptom: Pages on io-shop were slow to respond
